Researchers have already isolated some strains of these zombie viruses and demonstrated that they are still capable of infecting host cells, even though they have been buried in permafrost for thousands of years. These viruses could infect humans with diseases from the distant past that our immune systems may have never encountered, and that could be resistant to current treatments [4]. Therefore, these viruses represent a potential pandemic threat that needs to be monitored and controlled.

The aim of this short article is to provide an overview of the current state of knowledge on the zombie viruses, their origin, diversity, infectivity, and impact on human health and the environment along with the challenges and opportunities for monitoring, prevention, and control of these emerging pathogens, as well as the role of social media and public education in raising awareness and combating misinformation. ORIGIN, DIVERSITY, AND INFECTIVITY The term zombie virus refers to viruses that have been inactive for a long time, but could be revived by environmental changes. The term is also used in fiction to describe a pathogen that transforms humans into undead creatures that spread the infection by biting. It is a metaphor for the unknown and the mysterious in infectious disease fiction, as well as an allegory of a communicable disease that serve as a symbol of the sick or the disease in their horde-like behaviour and reveals the patterns of contagion and the disaster among communities. The origin of the zombie viruses is not clear, but scientists believe that they may have been frozen in the permafrost during the last ice age, which lasted from about 2.6 million years ago to about 11,700 years ago. During this period, the Earth experienced several cycles of glacial and interglacial periods, which affected the climate, the sea level, and the distribution of life forms. The permafrost formed as a result of the accumulation of snow and ice that did not melt during the summer, and that preserved the organic matter and the microorganisms that were trapped within it. The permafrost may contain viruses that are up to a million years old and so will be far older than our own species, which is thought to have emerged about 300,000 years ago [6]. “Our immune systems may have never been in contact with some of those microbes, and that is another worry,” said Jean-Michel Claverie, a geneticist from Aix-Marseille University who has been studying the zombie viruses [7]. The diversity of the zombie viruses is also unknown, but researchers have identified several different viral strains from various sites in Siberia and other regions of the Arctic. These viruses belong to different families and genera, such as Pandoravirus, Pithovirus, Megavirus, and Pacmanvirus, which are among the largest and most complex viruses known to science. They have genomes that range from 500,000 to 2.5 million base pairs, which is larger than some bacteria and archaea, along with some unique morphological features, such as icosahedral or amphora-shaped capsids, and unusual replication cycles, such as infecting the host cell nucleus or forming viral factories in the cytoplasm. These viruses are mainly found to infect single-celled organisms, such as amoebae, which are abundant and diverse in the permafrost. However, some of these viruses may also have the potential to infect multicellular organisms, such as plants, animals, and humans. For example, researchers have detected genomic traces of poxviruses and herpesviruses, which are well known human pathogens, in some of the permafrost samples. In 2018, researchers recovered microscopic nematode worms that were frozen in Siberian soil for 42,000 years. The researchers confirmed that the animals that moved and ate after being placed in nutrient-rich Petri dishes at 20 °C were not contaminated samples [8]. The infectivity of the zombie viruses is also uncertain, but researchers have demonstrated that some of them are still able to infect host cells after being frozen for thousands of years. For example, Claverie and his team isolated a virus that was 48,500 years old from a permafrost sample in Siberia, and showed that it could still infect an amoeba species called Acanthamoeba castellanii [7]. This virus, named Pandoravirus yedoma, is the oldest frozen virus to become infectious. It is older than the 30,000-year-old virus identified in Siberia in 2013, which was also isolated by Claverie's team [7]. The researchers used Acanthamoeba as a virus bait, as it is a common host for many large viruses. They also used strict biosafety measures to prevent contamination and spread of the viruses to the laboratory workers and the environment which emphasized that the viruses they isolated were only able to infect amoebae and posed no risk to humans. However, they warned that other viruses, currently frozen in the permafrost, might be able to trigger illnesses in humans. “We have to assume that something like this could happen,” said Dr. Marion Koopmans, a virologist from the Erasmus Medical Center in Rotterdam who has been collaborating with Claverie [9]. To investigate the diversity and function of these ancient viruses, a team of researchers led by Dr. Lonnie Thompson and Dr. Matthew Sullivan from Ohio State University conducted a metagenomic analysis of two ice core samples collected from the Guliya ice cap on the Tibetan Plateau, which is located at an altitude of 6.7 kilometers and has an estimated age of 15,000 years [10]. The researchers used a combination of advanced techniques, such as sterile drilling, decontamination, and ultra-low temperature processing, to minimize the risk of contamination and preserve the integrity of the samples. The team found that the ice cores contained a rich and diverse viral community, with 33 viral populations identified, of which 28 were novel and had no close relatives in the public databases [10]. They then compared the viral genomes to those of known viruses and inferred their possible hosts and functions which allowed them to discover that the most abundant viruses in both samples were bacteriophages that infect Methylobacterium, a genus of bacteria that plays a key role in the methane cycle within ice. These phages showed high similarity to those found in Methylobacterium strains from plant and soil habitats, suggesting that they originated from terrestrial sources and were transported to the ice cap by dust and wind [10]. The researchers also found that these phages had genes that could enhance the nutrient uptake and metabolism of their hosts, indicating that they had a mutualistic relationship with the bacteria which enabled them to also characterize the novel viruses and find that they had unique features that enabled them to survive and infect cells in extreme cold environments. These features included signatures of genes that encode for cold-shock proteins, antifreeze proteins, ice-nucleation proteins, and cold-adapted enzymes. It was speculated that these viruses were adapted to the harsh conditions of the ice cap and could infect psychrophilic (coldloving) microorganisms. The researchers concluded that these ancient viruses provide a valuable window into the past atmospheric and environmental conditions, as well as the evolutionary history of viruses. They also warned that the melting of the ice cap could pose a potential threat to the current biosphere, as some of the viruses may be able to infect humans or other animals. This calls for more research and surveillance on the emerging viruses from the permafrost, as they may have unpredictable consequences for the global health and ecology.

. For example, in 2016, an anthrax outbreak occurred in Siberia, killing more than 2,300 reindeer and infecting dozens of people, including a 12-year-old boy who died [6]. The outbreak was linked to the thawing of a reindeer carcass that was infected with anthrax and buried in the permafrost for decades. The carcass was exposed by the melting of the permafrost and the rising of the water level, and the anthrax spores were dispersed by the wind and the water. The outbreak was also facilitated by the high density and the movement of the reindeer herds, as well as the lack of vaccination and the delay in the diagnosis and the treatment of the infected people and animals. The outbreak was contained by the intervention of the authorities, who vaccinated the reindeer and the people, and burned the carcasses and the contaminated soil [6]. This was a wake-up call for the potential dangers of permafrost thawing and the need for preparedness and prevention.
